name: Flu (influenza)
definition: Flu is a respiratory illness caused by influenza viruses.
overview: Flu is an infection of the airways caused by influenza viruses. It comes on very quickly, with a sudden high temperature, aching body, tiredness, dry cough, sore throat and headache. Most people recover at home, but flu can lead to complications such as bronchitis and pneumonia, and older adults, pregnant women, young children and people with long-term conditions face a higher risk. Yearly vaccination is the main recommended protection.
causes: Infection with influenza viruses; types A and B cause the seasonal epidemics seen in people.
The virus spreads mainly in droplets made when people with flu cough, sneeze or talk.
Touching a contaminated surface and then the face is a less common route.
The NHS says germs from coughs and sneezes can live on hands and surfaces for 24 hours.
riskFactors: Long-term conditions such as asthma, diabetes or heart disease
signs: A high temperature with aching and a dry cough, which other viruses can also cause
complications: Inflammation of the heart or brain
In severe cases, hospital admission or death
diagnosis: Clinicians often diagnose flu from the typical symptoms, and a swab test can confirm it. Symptoms alone cannot say for certain, because other viruses cause a similar illness. Quick tests exist, although some are less accurate than laboratory tests.
treatment: Most people recover at home with rest, fluids and over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen. Antibiotics do not work on flu because it is a viral illness. Antiviral medicines can be prescribed for people at high risk or who are very sick, and work best when started early. The NHS says aspirin should not be given to children under 16.
prevention: Annual vaccination is the main recommended protection, alongside regular handwashing and covering coughs and sneezes. UKHSA says the vaccine is updated every year because the virus changes.
seekCare: Call 999 or go to A&E for sudden chest pain, severe difficulty breathing or coughing up blood. Contact NHS 111 or a GP the same day when the person is 65 or over, pregnant, has a long-term condition or a weakened immune system, feels very unwell or short of breath, or has not improved after 7 days. Milder illness is usually managed at home.

sections.heading: What are the symptoms of flu, and how is it different from a cold?
sections.body:
The NHS describes flu as an illness that comes on very quickly. Typical features include a sudden high temperature, an aching body, tiredness, a dry cough, a sore throat and a headache. Compared with a cold, flu leaves people exhausted and too unwell to carry on as normal.

Hospital leaflets that follow NHS advice describe a cold as building up gradually, with a runny nose, sneezing and watery eyes. Flu usually starts more suddenly, tends to be more severe and lasts longer than a cold. Fever and body aches are more often part of flu. Tiredness can linger after other symptoms ease, and a cough may last a week or so longer. Because other viruses cause similar illnesses, the symptoms alone cannot prove that someone has flu.

sections.heading: How does flu spread?
sections.body:
Flu is caused by influenza viruses. The CDC describes four types, but only types A and B cause the seasonal epidemics seen in people. Type A viruses are divided into subtypes such as H1N1 and H3N2, while type B viruses are split into two lineages.

Most experts think flu spreads mainly through droplets made when people with the infection cough, sneeze or talk. The NHS says coughs and sneezes spread the germs, which can live on hands and surfaces for 24 hours. Touching a contaminated surface and then the face is thought to be a less common route. The CDC says the virus can be found in most infected people from one day before symptoms start and for five to seven days after they become ill. People are most contagious during the first three days of the illness.

sections.heading: How is flu diagnosed, and how long does it last?
sections.body:
Clinicians often diagnose flu from the typical symptoms, and a swab test can confirm it. Other viruses cause a similar illness, so symptoms alone cannot settle the question. Quick tests exist, although some are less accurate than laboratory tests.

The CDC says most people can recover from flu at home without medical care. One NHS hospital leaflet describes flu in otherwise healthy people as unpleasant but usually self-limiting, with recovery within 2 to 7 days. Other NHS leaflets put recovery at about a week. They add that tiredness can last longer than the other symptoms. Symptoms that become more severe or last longer than about a week are a reason to seek medical advice.

sections.heading: What is the treatment for flu?
sections.body:
Most people recover at home with rest, plenty of fluids and over-the-counter pain relief such as paracetamol or ibuprofen. NHS hospital leaflets add that keeping warm and drinking enough water helps avoid dehydration. Antibiotics do not work on flu, because it is caused by a virus. The NHS says aspirin should not be given to children under 16.

Antiviral medicines can be prescribed for people at high risk or who are very sick. They work best when started early, within about two days of symptoms beginning. The CDC says antiviral treatment matters most for people at high risk, and can make the difference between a milder illness and a very serious one that ends in hospital. An NHS trust leaflet says antivirals are generally not recommended for otherwise healthy adults.

sections.heading: What are the complications of flu, and when should someone get medical help?
sections.body:
Most flu passes without lasting problems, but complications happen. The NHS lists bronchitis, pneumonia, sinus and ear infections, and inflammation of the heart or brain. UKHSA adds that flu can make existing health conditions worse and, in severe cases, lead to hospital admission or death. Older adults, pregnant women, young children and people with long-term conditions such as asthma, diabetes or heart disease are at higher risk. The CDC also says even healthy children and adults can become very ill with flu.

For urgent concerns, the NHS advises contacting NHS 111 or the GP the same day when the person is 65 or over, pregnant, or has a long-term condition or weakened immune system. The same applies when someone feels very unwell or short of breath, or has not improved after 7 days. Sudden chest pain, severe difficulty breathing or coughing up blood are reasons to call 999 or go to A&E.

sections.heading: Who is offered the flu vaccine, and what else helps prevent flu?
sections.body: Annual flu vaccination is the main recommended protection, alongside regular handwashing and covering coughs and sneezes. UKHSA says the vaccine is updated every year because the flu virus changes. UKHSA's guide to the autumn 2026 programme lists pregnant women, children, people aged 65 and over, and people in clinical risk groups among those eligible. It also includes residents of long-stay care homes, close contacts of people with a weakened immune system, and some frontline social care workers. The clinical risk groups include chronic respiratory disease such as asthma and COPD, chronic heart disease, chronic kidney disease, chronic liver disease, diabetes and a weakened immune system. Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland follow their own health departments' guidance.

faqs.q: Is flu the same as a cold?
faqs.a: They are different illnesses. Flu usually starts suddenly, tends to be more severe and lasts longer than a cold. The NHS says flu leaves people exhausted and too unwell to carry on as normal. A cold tends to build up gradually and often brings a runny nose and sneezing. Fever and body aches are more often linked with flu.

No, because flu is caused by a virus and antibiotics act on bacteria. Antiviral medicines can be prescribed for people at high risk or who are very sick. They work best when started early, within about two days of symptoms starting. Most people recover with rest, fluids and simple pain relief.

faqs.q: How long is someone contagious with flu?
faqs.a: The CDC says the virus can be detected in most infected people from one day before symptoms develop. It can still be detected for five to seven days after they become sick. People are most contagious in the first three days of illness. The CDC describes the main route as droplets from coughing, sneezing and talking.

faqs.q: Who is most at risk of serious illness from flu?
faqs.a: Older adults, pregnant women, young children and people with long-term conditions such as asthma, diabetes or heart disease are at higher risk of complications. People with a weakened immune system are also included in UKHSA's clinical risk groups. The CDC adds that even healthy children and adults can get very sick from flu.

faqs.q: When does flu need emergency help?
faqs.a: The NHS advises calling 999 or going to A&E for sudden chest pain, severe difficulty breathing or coughing up blood. Contact with NHS 111 or the GP the same day is advised for people aged 65 or over, who are pregnant, or who have a long-term condition or weakened immune system. The same route applies to anyone who feels very unwell or short of breath, or has not improved after 7 days.
